title: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The domestic horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra are descended from a common ancestor that was striped like a zebra, which explains the occasional appearance of stripes in horses, asses and their hybrids.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For myself, I venture confidently to look back thousands on thousands of generations, and I see an animal striped like a zebra, but perhaps otherwise very differently constructed, the common parent of our domestic horse, whether or not it be descended from one or more wild stocks, of the ass, the hemionus, quagga, and zebra.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Reversions to long-lost characters.”. Scope: genus Equus

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Common ancestry is strongly testable, and ancestral striping can be probabilistically reconstructed. Direct evidence for the ancestral phenotype remains incomplete, so the full historical claim is not decisively resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Infer Equus relationships and reconstruct ancestral coat-pattern states using ancient and modern genomes, preserved pigmentation loci, fossil evidence and extant phenotype coding. A common ancestor with high posterior support for striping supports the claim; independent stripe origins or a confidently unstriped ancestor refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Coat stripes are rarely preserved in fossils.

Ancient DNA does not reach the deepest Equus common ancestor and pigmentation genotype-phenotype mapping is incomplete.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.82
discriminating power: 0.67

analysis feasibility: 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The genus is small, densely sequenced, and includes ancient DNA, so monophyly of the named equids is decidable with public genomes and standard methods. Whether their common ancestor was striped like a zebra is a low-powered reconstruction of a labile trait, and an equivocal result would leave that clause unresolved. The data therefore settle the genealogical part more cleanly than the historical colour pattern.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate the phylogeny of living and recently extinct equids from genomes and reconstruct the striping state of their common ancestor. A single clade whose ancestor is reconstructed as striped would confirm the claim; an unstriped ancestor, or striping confined to nested zebra lineages, would refute the striped-parent clause. Common ancestry itself is a separate and sharper test than the stripe reconstruction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Partial leg and shoulder stripes in horses and asses can be coded in more than one way.

The phenotype of stem equids is inferred rather than observed.

Striping is evolutionarily labile, so ancestral-state reconstruction can be equivocal.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.76
analysis feasibility: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.58
data existence: 0.88
